title: Light continues to echo three years after stellar outburst
caption: The light echo around V838 Monocerotis, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, and The Hubble Heritage Team (AURA/STScI)

recognition.text: Ranked #26 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble image shows the star V838 Monocerotis, or V838 Mon, surrounded by dusty clouds whose lighting has changed greatly. The effect is known as a light echo.

In early 2002 the star suddenly brightened for several weeks. The flash of light then traveled outward through the dust around the star. Because light takes time to cross space, it reaches different parts of the cloud at different times, and each part lights up as the flash passes through and reflects some of it toward us. The result is like a sonar sweep that gradually lights up the surroundings layer by layer.

That is why the view keeps changing. Ever since the outburst, the echo has been revealing dust patterns that had never been seen before, as the light reaches ever more distant parts of the cloud. Hubble's repeated images let astronomers watch that process unfold. The official caption offers few other details.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the reflected light from the dust is far too faint to see without a long telescope exposure.
